questions.stem: What is plotted on the y-axis of an energy level diagram?

options.text: The energy of the reactants and products
options.explanation: The vertical axis carries the energy levels whose gap gives the enthalpy change.

options.text: The progress of the reaction
options.explanation: Progress runs along the x-axis; energy sits on the y-axis.

options.text: The temperature of the mixture
options.explanation: Temperature belongs to thermometer readings, not to this diagram.

options.text: The rate of the reaction
options.explanation: Rate graphs are a different topic with different axes.

questions.stem: Which arrow direction marks an endothermic reaction on an energy level diagram?

options.text: Upwards, because the products end higher than the reactants
options.explanation: Energy taken in leaves the products on a higher level, so the arrow climbs.

options.text: Downwards, because the mixture cools
options.explanation: The cooling of the surroundings is not what the arrow tracks; the product level is higher.

options.text: Horizontal, because energy is conserved
options.explanation: Conservation governs total energy, not the levels drawn for the chemicals.

options.text: It depends on the temperature of the room
options.explanation: The arrow follows the chemistry, not the surroundings.

questions.stem: What does the vertical gap between the reactant and product levels represent?

options.text: The overall enthalpy change of the reaction
options.explanation: The height difference is exactly the energy change the diagram is built to show.

options.text: The activation energy of the reaction
options.explanation: Activation energy appears on reaction profiles, not on simple energy level diagrams.

options.text: The time the reaction takes
options.explanation: Time never appears on an energy level diagram.

options.text: The temperature rise recorded by a thermometer
options.explanation: Thermometer data is experimental; the gap is the energy difference.

questions.stem: In an exothermic energy level diagram, where do the products sit?

options.text: Below the reactants, because energy was given out
options.explanation: Released energy leaves the products on a lower level than the reactants.

options.text: Above the reactants, because the mixture warmed
options.explanation: Warming the surroundings does not lift the product level; giving out energy lowers it.

options.text: On the same level as the reactants
options.explanation: Equal levels would mean no enthalpy change at all.

options.text: Off the diagram, because products are unstable
options.explanation: Products sit firmly on their own level however stable they are.

questions.stem: A diagram shows the product level above the reactant level. What does it depict?

options.text: An endothermic reaction with a positive enthalpy change
options.explanation: Higher products mean energy was taken in, which is the endothermic signature.

options.text: An exothermic reaction with a negative enthalpy change
options.explanation: Exothermic reactions place products lower, not higher.

options.text: A reaction with no energy change
options.explanation: A level difference always signals an energy change.

options.text: An incomplete reaction waiting for more energy
options.explanation: The diagram describes the energy bookkeeping, not the completion state.

questions.stem: Which axis carries the energy scale in an energy level diagram, and what does the other axis track?
questions.modelAnswer: Energy is plotted up the vertical axis, while the horizontal axis tracks how far the reaction has progressed.

questions.stem: State the direction of the arrow on an energy level diagram for an exothermic change.
questions.modelAnswer: The arrow points downwards for exothermic reactions and upwards for endothermic ones.

questions.stem: Explain what the height difference between the reactant and product levels shows on an energy level diagram.
questions.modelAnswer: The height difference represents the overall enthalpy change of the reaction, showing how much energy the products hold relative to the reactants.

questions.stem: A diagram shows the reactant level below the product level. State the type of reaction drawn and justify it.
questions.modelAnswer: Reactants sitting below the products shows an endothermic reaction, because energy has been taken in to raise the product level.

questions.stem: Which set of features must every energy level diagram carry?

options.text: Labelled axes, named energy levels and a directed arrow
options.explanation: Those three elements let the reader extract the reaction type and the enthalpy change.

options.text: A curve through the transition state
options.explanation: Curves and peaks belong to reaction profiles, not energy level diagrams.

options.text: Time intervals along the x-axis
options.explanation: The x-axis carries reaction progress, not time.

options.text: The temperature values measured
options.explanation: Experimental temperatures are not part of the diagram.

questions.stem: What sign belongs to the enthalpy change in the sketch with products below reactants?

options.text: Negative, because energy left the chemicals
options.explanation: A drop in level means energy was released, which is written as a negative change.

options.text: Positive, because the products are stable
options.explanation: Stability is not the sign rule; the direction of energy flow is.

options.text: Zero, because the arrow is short
options.explanation: Arrow length is a drawing choice, not the sign.

options.text: The sign depends on the fuel used
options.explanation: The placement of the levels fixes the sign whatever the chemicals.

questions.stem: A student draws an exothermic diagram but points the arrow upwards. What should be corrected?

options.text: The arrow, which must point downwards from reactants to products
options.explanation: Exothermic changes lose energy, so the arrow descends to the lower product level.

options.text: Nothing: exothermic arrows point upwards
options.explanation: Upward arrows mark endothermic changes only.

options.text: The axes, which should swap places
options.explanation: The axes are correct; only the arrow direction is wrong.

options.text: The reaction type, which must be endothermic
options.explanation: The student intends an exothermic sketch; the drawing, not the intent, needs fixing.

questions.stem: Why does the endothermic sketch carry a positive enthalpy change?

options.text: Energy is taken in, so the products end with more energy than the reactants
options.explanation: Gaining energy raises the product level and gives the change its positive sign.

options.text: Because the thermometer reads a higher number
options.explanation: Endothermic reactions make the thermometer fall; the sign comes from the energy flow.

options.text: Because the products are heavier
options.explanation: Mass has no role in the energy levels.

options.text: Positive signs are used for all sketches
options.explanation: Exothermic sketches are negative by the same convention.

questions.stem: How can you identify the reaction type from a finished, labelled diagram?

options.text: Compare the reactant and product levels and note the arrow direction
options.explanation: Relative levels plus arrow direction give the type immediately.

options.text: Measure the length of the x-axis
options.explanation: The x-axis carries progress and its length means nothing.

options.text: Count the labels written on the diagram
options.explanation: Label count is a quality check, not a type test.

options.text: Check whether the diagram is drawn in pencil
options.explanation: Drawing medium has no chemical meaning.

questions.stem: State how the reactant and product levels are arranged in the exothermic sketch.
questions.modelAnswer: The exothermic sketch shows reactants high, products low and a downward arrow between the two levels.

questions.stem: State the sign of the enthalpy change in the endothermic sketch.
questions.modelAnswer: The enthalpy change is positive for the endothermic sketch and negative for the exothermic one.

questions.stem: Explain why both energy level sketches need labelled axes and named levels.
questions.modelAnswer: Labelled axes and named energy levels make the direction of energy change unambiguous, so a reader can tell exothermic from endothermic at a glance and the sketch carries the chemistry.

questions.stem: A reaction mixture cools from 21 degrees Celsius to 17 degrees Celsius as it reacts. State whether energy is given out or taken in, and classify the change.
questions.modelAnswer: The temperature fall shows energy is taken in from the surroundings by the reaction, so the change is endothermic.
